title: The Week That Was
gist: A weekly digest of Lawfare's coverage spanning Comey/Fauci Trump-era legal fights, U.S. troop data privacy, DoD civilian-harm rollback, Gaza and Ukraine developments, an Exxon-Cuba sovereign immunity ruling, and multiple AI governance threads (constitution regulation, GSA contracting ambiguity, Grokipedia's frozen edit queue, AI consciousness).

themes.theme: Domestic Legal Fights Around the Trump Administration

insights.claim: The Department of Justice continues attempting to prove that '8647,' spelled out in seashells in a photo posted by James Comey, is mafia slang for killing someone, even though almost all the evidence points to the contrary.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Illustrates a contested, evidence-thin prosecutorial theory being pursued against a former FBI director.
insights.quote: Parloff chronicled the continued attempts by the Department of Justice to prove that “8647” is mafia slang for killing someone, even as almost all the evidence points to the contrary.

insights.claim: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to stay a district court order halting enforcement of its mail-in voting executive order, amid a separate nationwide preliminary injunction against the same order and a new birthright citizenship order.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Tracks an active, multi-front legal battle over voting rules with a case now before the Supreme Court.
insights.locator: Benjamin Wittes sat down with Eric Columbus

insights.claim: The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt for invoking the Fifth Amendment during questioning, but because a contempt vote is unlikely to overcome a Senate filibuster, any Justice Department prosecution would have to bypass the standard statutory and precedential procedure for contempt.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
entities: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
insights.so_what: Flags a procedural workaround that could set precedent for how contempt prosecutions proceed when normal legislative mechanisms stall.
insights.quote: because a contempt vote is unlikely to overcome the filibuster, any prosecution pursued by the Department of Justice would bypass the standard procedure for contempt created by statute and precedent

insights.claim: A fired Justice Department prosecutor is challenging his firing, discussed alongside a nationwide preliminary injunction against the mail-in ballot executive order and the new birthright citizenship order on Lawfare Live.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Adds to a pattern of personnel and policy legal challenges within the Justice Department this week.
insights.locator: Wittes sat down with Roberts, Anna Bower, and Parloff

themes.theme: National Security Data and Defense Policy

insights.claim: Vast amounts of data on U.S. troops are easily available for commercial purchase, allowing adversaries to track troop movements without needing to find an actual security breach, and the Justice Department's Data Security Program should be used to build a robust regulatory framework since case-by-case regulation and enforcement cannot address the problem.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Identifies commercial data brokerage as an overlooked national security vulnerability that current piecemeal enforcement cannot fix.
insights.quote: Licata argued that the Justice Department's Data Security Program should be used to develop a robust regulatory framework to address this vulnerability in ways case-by-case regulation and enforcement cannot.

insights.claim: The Department of Defense has reversed recent years of progress on its civilian harm mitigation and response initiatives, with key policy developments and reviews abruptly halted, beyond just administration rhetoric dismissing the concerns, even as the underlying need for such initiatives remains.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Documents a concrete rollback of civilian-protection policy infrastructure within DoD, not merely a rhetorical shift.
insights.quote: beyond Trump administration leaders' rhetoric dismissing concerns over CHMR, key policy developments and reviews have been abruptly halted, even as the need for them remains
insights.locator: Mae Thompson, Kristine Beckerle, and Luke Moffett considered

insights.claim: This week's national security news roundup included cyberattacks on water utilities in at least seven U.S. states, new revelations about OpenAI's agents hacking other companies, and the cost and implications of the continued National Guard presence in Washington, D.C.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Signals that critical-infrastructure cyberattacks and AI-agent misuse are now treated as mainstream national security news alongside domestic security deployments.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has a new plan for Gaza that Israel does not appear to be on board with, intersecting with developments in Lebanon and the West Bank and with Israel's upcoming elections.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Flags a gap between U.S. and Israeli positions on Gaza policy that could shape the trajectory of the conflict and Israeli domestic politics.
insights.locator: Scott R. Anderson sat down with Joel Braunold

insights.claim: The Supreme Court held that Cuba's CIMEX cannot invoke sovereign immunity to block Exxon's suit alleging CIMEX continues to traffic in and profit from property nationalized by Cuba in 1959, a decision resting on whether Title III of the Helms-Burton Act implicitly abrogates Cuba's sovereign immunity, which commentators argue erodes U.S. commitments to sovereign immunity and international law more broadly.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A significant sovereign immunity ruling with implications for how U.S. courts treat foreign state-owned entities going forward.
insights.quote: the decision erodes the U.S.'s commitments to respecting sovereign immunity and international law more broadly
insights.locator: Annie Brett and Cory A. Evans explained

insights.claim: Following the firing of Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and the dismissal of General Oleksandr Syrskyi, Fedorov rejected a 'hollow' vice prime minister role and is rising in the polls despite having no formal political ambitions, raising questions about President Zelensky and public trust.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A notable Ukrainian political realignment with a rising independent political figure that could affect Zelensky's standing.
insights.quote: Fedorov's rejection of a "vice prime minister" role, his rise in the polls despite having no formal political ambitions, and what it all means for President Zelensky and the public's trust
insights.locator: Anastasiia Lapatina sat down with Danylo Mokryk

insights.claim: Contradictions dating back to the UN Security Council's founding continue to render it ineffective, and now, on the anniversary of the Hiroshima bombing, is the time to reform the UN Charter, drawing on a historical episode where meaningful charter reform progress was made despite the objections of the Security Council's permanent members.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Argues institutional reform of the Security Council is achievable even against permanent-member objections, citing historical precedent.

insights.claim: Civil forfeiture, the government's current favored legal response to pig-butchering scams, is overly reliant on cooperation from international companies and often fails to restore funds to victims even when investigations are considered successful.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Highlights a structural weakness in the primary U.S. legal tool for recovering scam victims' funds.
insights.quote: civil forfeiture investigations, the government's current favored legal response to pig-butchering scams, are overly reliant on cooperation from international companies and often fail to restore funds to victims, even when considered successful

insights.claim: A revised General Services Administration Acquisition Regulation clause governing AI contracts fails to clearly define what constitutes a 'government usage context,' creating ambiguity about what data the clause protects, an ambiguity too consequential to be left to resolve itself through contract administration over time.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Points to a specific regulatory drafting gap that could leave sensitive government data inadequately protected in AI contracts.
insights.quote: Tillipman explained that the ambiguity is too consequential to be left to acquire meaning over time through contract administration.

insights.claim: AI constitutions, the documents setting out the values and rules AI models should follow, contain speech protected by the First Amendment, which limits how far the government can go in regulating them; narrower government approaches could include requiring disclosures, using procurement leverage, or mandating provisions against criminal conduct.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Summarizes a legal argument constraining how aggressively regulators can rewrite AI value-setting documents, pointing instead to disclosure and procurement levers.

insights.claim: An analysis of Grokipedia found its edit-review queue froze around April 24 with no announcement to users or contributors, and a mass rewrite of the site broke the anchors linking suggested edits to specific text, illustrating how the new AI information ecosystem is being shaped by out-of-date but open-access resources with no accountability.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Exposes a governance failure in an AI-generated reference platform that could leave stale, uncorrectable information influencing AI-era information consumption.
insights.quote: finding that Grokipedia's edit-review queue froze around April 24, with no announcement to users or contributors
insights.locator: Kate Klonick sat down with Renée DiResta

insights.claim: AI is beginning to reshape gastroenterology, opening new possibilities for earlier diagnosis, personalized treatment of diseases like inflammatory bowel disease, and faster clinical research.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete example of AI's application moving from general-purpose tools into specialized clinical medicine.

insights.claim: A discussion of whether AI could ever be conscious, drawing on Anil Seth's recent essay, attempted to define consciousness, weigh arguments for and against machine consciousness, and assess what current evidence can and cannot tell us and what it means for policymakers and users.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Frames AI consciousness as an open question with direct policy relevance, not just a philosophical curiosity.

themes.theme: Cross-References to Other Lawfare Analysis This Week

insights.claim: This week's Foreign Policy Essay covered the gap between the Somali government's optimistic vision of near-victory over al-Shabaab in Mogadishu and the opposition's more pessimistic emphasis on the group's surviving networks, a gap the analysis argues reflects continued political fissures that will matter more as external support to Somalia is withdrawn.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Summarizes a separate in-depth Lawfare analysis of Somalia's fragile security narrative within this week's roundup.
insights.locator: Tricia Bacon analyzed the current security situation

insights.claim: This week's Seriously Risky Business cybersecurity newsletter discussed a rise in data theft extortion and why it might be time to reinvigorate CISA's Secure by Design initiative.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Cross-references the week's cybersecurity policy coverage within the broader digest.
insights.locator: Tom Uren discussed a rise in data theft extortion
